newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Singh slams government on oil deficit.
newsitem.headline: India's Singh slams government on oil deficit.

text.p: Former Indian finance minister Manmohan Singh was quoted on Monday as saying that the government had stoked fears of inflation by not taking steps to curb a huge deficit arising out of subsidised oil prices.

Singh, the architect of India's economic reforms programme launched in 1991, sharply criticised Finance Minister P. Chidambaram for not raising petroleum product prices to contain the deficit incurred by state-controlled oil companies.
"The budget's failure in ignoring the oil pool deficit, I believe, creates an environment of uncertainty," Singh told the Economic Times newspaper in an interview.

He said fears of inflation fuelled by the deficit, currently around 160 billion rupees ($4.5 billion), could undo positive measures in Chidambaram's budget for 1997/98 (April-March), in which he proposed wide-ranging tax cuts welcomed by industry.

The budget's "other provisions seek to promote investment, but there is always this Damocles' sword hanging overhead...The failure to tackle the oil pool deficit stokes inflationary expectations," Singh was quoted as saying.
India's year-on-year inflation rate measured by wholesale prices is currently around 7.9 percent, compared with 4.5 percent a year ago.

Leading economists have criticised the government for not reducing the oil pool deficit, which arises out of state oil companies charging less than world prices for key fuels like diesel and kerosene.
The oil pool deficit shot up due to a rise in world oil prices last year. Singh said Chidambaram inherited a deficit of 50 billion rupees, which later widened.

Singh, the main economic ideologue of the Congress party, which offers make-or-break support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition, said inflationary expectations could also hurt export competitiveness.
He said the budget could attract foreign capital but inflation could hurt competitiveness and lead to a sudden flight of capital of the type Mexico witnessed in 1995.
"In the short run, I think, the Indian capital market will attract a lot of inflows. The rupee might even appreciate," Singh said.

"But sooner or later people would develop nervousness that the competitiveness of the country's exports would be compromised. With such fears around, a single shock can create a Mexico-like situation."

Singh also criticised the budget for proposing to cut the highest rate of personal income tax to 30 percent from 40 percent, saying it could even adversely affect the flow of concessional foreign aid to India.
"You can reduce (taxation) gradually. But you send the wrong signals when you slash the tax rates suddenly," Singh said.

Chidambaram was twice commerce minister in the previous Congress party government, and was part of a reforms team led by Singh. He joined a regional political party last year on the eve of general elections in which Congress was routed.
Chidambaram's regional party is one of the constitutents of the United Front coalition. ($1=35.8 rupees)
